When we round a decimal to the nearest whole number, we find the closest whole number to the original decimal.

[MATH: 16.4]

Content:
To round [MATH: 16.4] to the nearest whole number, we first identify the digit in the ones place:
[MATH: 1{\color{blue}{6}}.4]

Content:
We then look one digit to the right and compare it to the number [MATH: 5\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: 1{\color{blue}{6}}.\!{\color{red}{4}}]

Content:
Since [MATH: \color{red}4] is less than [MATH: 5], we round down. To do this, we remove all the digits to the right of the decimal point:

Content:
[MATH: 16.4 \rightarrow 16]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: 16.4] rounded to the nearest whole number is [MATH: 16.]

Content:
Some decimals have digits that continue forever.

Content:
For example, the number [MATH: \pi,] pronounced "pie," is a very important number in mathematics. Its digits continue forever, which we denote using [MATH: \ldots] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \pi= 3.141\,\ldots\,.]

Content:
Let's round this number to the nearest hundredth.

Content:
First, we locate the digit in the hundredths place:
[MATH: 3.1{\color{blue}{4}}1 \ldots]

Content:
We then look one digit to the right and compare it to the number [MATH: 5\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: 3.1{\color{blue}{4}}{\color{red}{1}} \ldots]

Content:
Since [MATH: \color{red}1] is less than [MATH: 5], we round down. To do this, we remove all digits to the right of the hundredths place:

Content:
[MATH: 3.141\ldots \rightarrow 3.14]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: \pi = 3.141\ldots] rounded to the nearest hundredth is [MATH: 3.14.]

Item 12 — Tutorial: Decimal Digits That Continue Forever

Content:
Some decimals have digits that continue forever.

Content:
For example, the number [MATH: \pi,] pronounced "pie," is a very important number in mathematics. Its digits continue forever, which we denote using [MATH: \ldots] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \pi= 3.141\,\ldots\,.]

Content:
Let's round this number to the nearest hundredth.

Content:
First, we locate the digit in the hundredths place:
[MATH: 3.1{\color{blue}{4}}1 \ldots]

Content:
We then look one digit to the right and compare it to the number [MATH: 5\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: 3.1{\color{blue}{4}}{\color{red}{1}} \ldots]

Content:
Since [MATH: \color{red}1] is less than [MATH: 5], we round down. To do this, we remove all digits to the right of the hundredths place:

Content:
[MATH: 3.141\ldots \rightarrow 3.14]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: \pi = 3.141\ldots] rounded to the nearest hundredth is [MATH: 3.14.]
